definition: In this historical psychology usage, the empirical method means investigating mind by starting with experience as it is actually found in consciousness, rather than assuming supposedly simple elements first and building upward from them. It begins with the fact that thought is occurring and analyzes it, instead of taking isolated sensations as the starting point.

provenance.scope: Source record fca72454f1995c69b072; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not explicitly state that the empirical method means “starting with experience as it is actually found in consciousness”; it only says that “Most books start with sensations… [which] is abandoning the empirical method of investigation,” and that the only allowable starting postulate is “the fact of thinking itself.”

The definition’s contrast “supposedly simple elements” and “building upward” is broadly consistent with the packet’s criticism of starting from “apparently innocent suppositions” about “sensations… the simplest things,” but the specific phrasing about starting with “supposedly simple elements” is not directly supported verbatim or as a directly stated formulation of the term.
